doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Baroque counterpoint, voice leading and bass lines in reharmonization
summary: Theory split from practice in classical music; Ellington, Strayhorn and Clare Fischer keep the original bass line when reharmonizing.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Let me backtrack just a second though. If you said this is not something that has a place in academia, isn’t the whole —

Well what I meant is that it’s not academic in the sense that, I mean the problem with classical music is that probably one of the reasons that improvisation died in classical music is that the theory became separated from the practice. So when Bach and the

Baroque composers were writing music and the music was contrapuntal, there was no system of harmony. People weren’t thinking about chord progressions in Bach’s time. All the Baroque music was composed and improvised in relation to melodic figures. And the composers and improvisers, first of all, everybody improvised then, because it was a part of the musical process, the musical common practice. And when Bach was writing inventions and fugues and things he wasn’t hearing a chord progression, he was starting with a musical figure and by imitation and different basic techniques of thematic development — thematic development and putting these figures together — what counterpoint is is basically developing musical figures in different degrees of density and contrapuntal textures in ways that sound harmonious. And so what happened later on is that Ramos and some of the theorists, because they thought some of this music sounded so great, they tried to figure out why it sounded good. And that’s when they came up with the basic theory of tonal harmony and common tone progressions. But what really makes counterpoint work, and what also makes the music that came after that that’s differently textured, instead of contrapuntal lines you have a single note melody and chords that provide a kind of harmonic accompaniment. The difference between a Bach fugue and a Mozart or Beethoven sonata is that in both of those things it’s primarily voice leading the principle, and the basic principle of voice leading that makes the music convincing. It’s just that in counterpoint all the voices in the voice leading texture are independently melodic, whereas in a more so-called homophonic texture where you get a melody and a harmonic accompaniment the harmony has a simpler kind of counterpoint. It’s basically half notes or whole notes working together. But just as the independent melodic counterpoint in Bach’s music made sense, the individual layers of the harmony in homophonic accompaniment make sense because of the voice leading. And then there’s also a more primary kind of voice leading that’s the relationship between the primary melody and these voices of harmony underneath, and even more so with the bass line. One of the things that I tell my students, whether you’re working on an arrangement for a group of horns or a big band, or whether you’re learning a tune as a vehicle for improvisation, is first pay attention to the melody in the bass line. And even when you’re doing a so-called re-harmonization, like one of the things I noticed when I started trying to transcribe things, whether it was pianists like Bill Evans or later on, one of my favorites, the biggest harmonic influence after Ellington and Strayhorn has been Clare Fischer. And both with Ellington and Strayhorn and Clare, when they arranged popular songs, standards from the American songbook, if you listen to the bass line that they use you will notice that it’s not all that different from the bass line in the original sheet music.
